title: HarmoniumClear
question: How does a harmonium work?
hook: Every note on a harmonium is a thin brass tongue buzzing through a slot, fed by air you pump with one hand. Take one apart in 3D, scrape a reed to tune it, pull the stops, hear why its fixed notes got it banned from All India Radio, and play it with your keyboard.

explainer.title: A box of reeds and a bellows
explainer.text: An Indian harmonium is a wooden box with a keyboard on top and a hinged bellows at the back. Inside sit a spring-loaded reservoir of air, a reed board with rows of brass reeds in little cells, a padded valve (a pallet) under every key, and stop knobs that choose which rows get air.

explainer.title: A brass tongue that chops the air
explainer.text: Each note is a free reed: a thin brass tongue riveted over a slot. Air pushes it through, it springs back, and every swing lets out a puff. It swings at its natural frequency, f = 0.56·(t/L²)·√(E/12ρ), so a longer tongue is much lower. Makers tune by scraping: the tip to go up, the root to go down.

explainer.title: Pump, store, squeeze
explainer.text: Your hand pushes air through a one-way valve into a reservoir held shut by springs. The springs keep the wind at about 0.5 to 1.5 kPa, only 1% above the room's pressure. Every open reed lets out about 0.07 L/s, so big chords drain it fast. Pump harder and it plays louder: that is its only volume control.

explainer.title: Pull a stop, add a voice
explainer.text: Each stop opens a bank of reeds: bass an octave down, male at the key's pitch, female an octave up. Their harmonics stack and beat gently, and a musette bank tuned a few cents sharp beats a few times a second. Drone stops hold Sa and Pa without any key.

explainer.title: Fixed notes in a sliding music
explainer.text: The reeds are tuned once, usually to equal temperament: Ga is 400 cents above Sa, while the pure 5/4 Ga that singers lean to is 386. Held together they beat about ten times a second. A scale changer slides the keyboard over the reeds to change key without changing fingers.

explainer.title: From church organ to every stage in India
explainer.text: Missionaries brought pedal reed organs; in Calcutta, Dwarkanath Ghose is widely credited with the hand-pumped floor harmonium by 1875. It spread to bhajan, kirtan, qawwali, theatre and film. All India Radio banned it from 1 March 1940, and partly lifted the ban in 1971. Masters like Tulsidas Borkar made it a solo voice.

concepts.def: A springy tongue that swings freely through a slot, chopping airflow into puffs. Used in harmoniums, accordions, harmonicas and the sheng.
The rate an object vibrates at by itself, set by its stiffness and its mass.
A beam fixed at one end and free at the other, like a diving board or a reed tongue.
The inner, spring-loaded bellows that stores air and keeps the wind pressure steady.
The padded valve under each key that lets air through that key's reeds.
A knob that opens or closes the air to one bank of reeds, or to a drone reed.
The slow swell and fade when two nearly equal frequencies sound together. The beat rate is their difference.
Tuning where every semitone is exactly 100 cents, so every key works but only octaves are pure.
A fine step of pitch in Indian music, finer than a semitone; tradition counts 22 in an octave.
